propositions.text: This is an application for judicial review of a RAD decision dated April 8, 2019.
propositions.quote: This is an application for judicial review of a Refugee Appeal Division [RAD] decision, dated April 8, 2019

propositions.text: The RAD decision concluded the Applicant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection under IRPA sections 96 and 97.
propositions.quote: that concluded that the Applicant is neither a Convention refugee under section 96 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 [IRPA], nor a person in need of protection under section 97 of the IRPA

paragraphs.summary: The court states this is a judicial review of a RAD decision denying the Applicant refugee or protection status under IRPA sections 96 and 97.

propositions.text: The RAD confirmed the RPD's finding that the Applicant had a viable Internal Flight Alternative in Islamabad, which was determinative.
propositions.quote: The RAD confirmed the findings of the Refugee Protection Division [RPD], in particular that the Applicant had a viable Internal Flight Alternative [IFA] in Islamabad (Pakistan), a finding that the RAD identified as determinative

paragraphs.summary: The RAD confirmed the RPD's finding that the Applicant had a viable Internal Flight Alternative in Islamabad, which was determinative.

propositions.text: The Applicant argues the RAD's discussion on the viability of the IFA was speculative about ongoing persecution threat.
propositions.quote: the Applicant argues that the RAD’s discussion as to the availability of a viable IFA was: (i) speculative as to the ongoing threat of persecution

propositions.text: The Applicant argues the RAD's discussion was incomplete as it failed to assess all factors under the second prong of the IFA test.
propositions.quote: and (ii) incomplete as it failed to assess the full range of factors under the second prong of the applicable test for an IFA

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues the RAD's IFA discussion was speculative and incomplete, failing to assess all relevant factors under the test.

propositions.text: The RAD's decision was not unreasonable and the application for judicial review is dismissed.
propositions.quote: I conclude that the RAD’s decision was not unreasonable. I, therefore, dismiss the application for judicial review

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the RAD decision was reasonable and dismisses the judicial review application.

propositions.text: The Applicant is a Pakistani citizen and drugstore owner in Sahiwal District, Punjab province.
propositions.quote: The Applicant is a citizen of Pakistan and the owner of a drugstore in the Sahiwal District. Sahiwal is located in the Punjab province of Pakistan

propositions.text: The Applicant is a licensed pharmacy technician who supplied free contraceptives to a nearby doctor.
propositions.quote: The Applicant is a trained pharmacy technician with a licence to sell drugs and narcotics. In addition to his regular business operations, the Applicant supplied free contraceptives to a nearby doctor

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant is a Pakistani citizen, licensed pharmacy technician, and drugstore owner who supplied free contraceptives to a doctor.

propositions.text: On August 15, 2016, unknown gang members threatened to kill the Applicant and family after he refused to supply bulk prescription medications.
propositions.quote: On August 15, 2016, a gang of unknown individuals came to the Applicant’s drugstore looking for prescription medications in bulk quantity. One of the individuals threatened to kill him and his family after the Applicant refused to supply them with the medicine

paragraphs.summary: The court recounts that on August 15, 2016, a gang threatened the Applicant and family after he refused to supply bulk medications.

propositions.text: On September 9, 2016, the Applicant was kidnapped, tortured, and threatened by the same gang demanding medications.
propositions.quote: On September 9, 2016, the Applicant was the victim of a kidnapping incident...the gang demanded that he provide them with certain medications

propositions.text: The Applicant escaped and filed a police report about the kidnapping incident.
propositions.quote: The Applicant was able to break away from the gang. He subsequently lodged a police report about the kidnapping incident

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant was kidnapped and tortured by the gang on September 9, 2016, escaped, and filed a police report.

propositions.text: On September 10 and 15, 2016, the Applicant was threatened by religious leaders and Taliban members to close his drugstore due to contraceptive sales.
propositions.quote: On September 10, 2016, the Applicant was threatened by a religious leader and certain members of the Taliban... On September 15, 2016, the Applicant was again threatened by another local religious leader and persons associated with the Taliban

propositions.text: Threats included death threats to the Applicant and his immediate family.
propositions.quote: During both of these incidents, they threatened to kill him and his immediate family

paragraphs.summary: The court recounts that the Applicant was threatened twice by religious leaders and Taliban members with death threats for selling contraceptives.

propositions.text: The Applicant closed his drugstore on September 16, 2016, and police refused to investigate after he contacted them on September 18.
propositions.quote: On September 16, 2016, he closed his drugstore. On September 18, 2016, the Applicant contacted the local police to conduct an investigation but they apparently refused to do so

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant closed his drugstore and police refused to investigate his threats.

propositions.text: The Applicant moved to Karachi, received threatening calls, and left Pakistan for Canada on October 20, 2016.
propositions.quote: The Applicant, along with his family, moved to Karachi...the Applicant received threatening phone calls... The Applicant then left his home country for Canada on October 20, 2016

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant moved to Karachi, received threats, and left Pakistan for Canada on October 20, 2016.

propositions.text: The Applicant claimed refugee status on November 30, 2016, recounting threats and an affidavit about unknown persons searching for him in January 2017.
propositions.quote: On November 30, 2016, the Applicant claimed refugee status...unknown persons came to the village of Sahiwal searching for the Applicant on January 7, 2017

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant claimed refugee status recounting threats and an affidavit about persons searching for him in January 2017.

propositions.text: The Applicant's refugee claim was transferred to the RPD, which held a hearing on June 15, 2017, and rejected the claim on June 30, 2017.
propositions.quote: His claim for refugee protection was transferred to the RPD. The RPD held a hearing on June 15, 2017, and rejected his claim on June 30, 2017

paragraphs.summary: The court states the RPD held a hearing and rejected the Applicant's refugee claim in June 2017.

propositions.text: The court will set out the RPD decision in detail despite the review being of the RAD decision.
propositions.quote: Although the decision before me on review is that of the RAD, I think it is important in this case to also set out in some detail the decision of the RPD

paragraphs.summary: The court explains it will detail the RPD decision even though the review concerns the RAD decision.

propositions.text: The RPD found the Applicant's credibility determinative, noting omissions, contradictions, vagueness, and evasiveness in testimony.
propositions.quote: The RPD concluded that the Applicant’s credibility was determinative in the case; in particular, the RPD found that there were omissions and contradictions in the Applicant’s testimony as compared with his BOC, that his testimony was vague and evasive

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found the Applicant's credibility determinative, noting omissions, contradictions, and evasiveness in his testimony.

propositions.text: The RPD did not believe the Applicant was threatened as claimed and found he failed to prove risk of danger under IRPA section 97(1).
propositions.quote: the RPD did not believe that the Applicant was threatened by those he claims...or that those incidents actually took place...failed to meet his burden to demonstrate...that he would be personally subjected to the danger or the risk provided for in subsection 97(1) of the IRPA

paragraphs.summary: The RPD disbelieved the Applicant's threats claims and found he failed to prove risk under IRPA section 97(1).

propositions.text: The RPD found that even if the Applicant was assaulted and threatened, he had a viable IFA in Islamabad.
propositions.quote: even if it had accepted that the Applicant had been assaulted and threatened as he claims, the Applicant nonetheless had a viable IFA in Islamabad

propositions.text: The RPD reasoned the threats arose from refusal to supply medications and contraceptives, but closure of the drugstore ended the risk.
propositions.quote: the threats made to the Applicant were as a result of his refusal to provide the assailants with the medication they demanded...with the closure of his drugstore, the activity that placed him at risk no longer exists

propositions.text: The RPD found no evidence the assailants would pursue the Applicant to Islamabad or that he would have difficulty settling there.
propositions.quote: The Applicant has not demonstrated that his assailants would still have an interest in pursuing him, and more so, so strong a willingness to pursue him to Islamabad...no evidence to suggest the Applicant would have difficulty travelling to Islamabad or settling down in that city

propositions.text: The RPD cited the National Documentation Package for Pakistan and noted the Applicant is a successful, educated businessman who travelled to Karachi.
propositions.quote: (The RPD cites the National Documentation Package for Pakistan ); and b) there is no evidence to suggest the Applicant would have difficulty travelling to Islamabad or settling down in that city in a reasonable manner. He is a successful, university-educated businessman who, according to his BOC, had travelled to Karachi and started to earn his livelihood

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found the threats ended with drugstore closure, no pursuit to Islamabad, and the Applicant could settle there as a successful businessman.

propositions.text: The Applicant appealed the RPD decision to the RAD.
propositions.quote: The Applicant then filed an appeal from the RPD decision before the RAD

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant appealed the RPD decision to the RAD.

propositions.text: The Applicant argued to the RAD that the RPD erred in credibility and IFA findings.
propositions.quote: the Applicant argued, amongst other things, that the RPD erred in its credibility finding as regards the Applicant, and that it also erred in the determination of a viable IFA

propositions.text: The Applicant did not present new evidence or request a RAD hearing.
propositions.quote: The Applicant did not present any new evidence, nor did he request a hearing before the RAD

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argued the RPD erred on credibility and IFA to the RAD but presented no new evidence or hearing request.

propositions.text: The Applicant argued the IFA determination was made in a factual vacuum or false premise and that assailants could track him, without elaboration.
propositions.quote: the Applicant suggested only that the determination of a viable IFA was made in a factual vacuum, or was at least based upon a false premise, and that the Applicant provided evidence that his assailants were willing and able to track him down, without elaborating any further

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argued the IFA finding was made in a factual vacuum or false premise and assailants could track him, without elaboration.

propositions.text: The RAD found the only determinative issue was the RPD's IFA evaluation and did not discuss credibility issues.
propositions.quote: the only determinative issue was whether the RPD had erred in its evaluation of the IFA, and thus it was unnecessary to discuss the issues pertaining to the credibility of the Applicant

propositions.text: The RAD concluded the RPD adequately addressed the IFA issue and dismissed the appeal.
propositions.quote: The RAD concluded that the RPD had adequately addressed that issue, and thus dismissed the appeal

paragraphs.summary: The RAD found the IFA evaluation determinative, did not discuss credibility, and dismissed the appeal as RPD addressed IFA adequately.

propositions.text: Whether the RAD erred in finding Islamabad offers a viable IFA is the only issue argued before me by the Applicant.
propositions.quote: The only issue argued before me by the Applicant was whether the RAD committed a reviewable error in finding that Islamabad offers a viable IFA.

propositions.text: Applicant did not raise issue of RAD not ruling on RPD's credibility finding, focusing only on RAD decision's IFA viability finding.
propositions.quote: The Applicant did not raise the issue of the RAD not ruling on the credibility finding of the RPD. The Applicant focused only on the RAD decision, which made it clear that, given its finding on the viability of the IFA, a discussion of the RPD’s credibility finding was not necessary.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues only that RAD erred in finding Islamabad a viable IFA and did not raise RAD's failure to rule on RPD credibility.

propositions.text: Suggests RAD should address RPD credibility findings in future to avoid unreasonable IFA analysis and remands.
propositions.quote: in the future, in similar circumstances, the RAD may wish to address the credibility findings of the RPD, so as to avoid a situation where an IFA analysis is found by this Court to be unreasonable, and necessarily determinative solely on account of the lack of any analysis on credibility, which may then require the return of the file to the RAD for the sole purpose of a complete analysis with regard to credibility.

paragraphs.summary: Court suggests RAD should address RPD credibility findings in future to avoid remands for incomplete analysis.

propositions.text: Vavilov sets presumption of reasonableness standard of review, rebuttable by clear legislative intent or questions of law of central importance.
propositions.quote: In Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 [Vavilov], the Supreme Court set out a revised framework for determining the applicable standard of review for administrative decisions. The starting point is a presumption that a standard of reasonableness applies (Vavilov at para 23). This presumption can be rebutted in the presence of (1) a clear legislative intention to prescribe a different standard of review, or (2) the types of questions in which the rule of law requires the application of the standard of correctness, such as constitutional question, questions of law of central importance to the legal system, and questions regarding the jurisdictional boundaries between administrative bodies (Vavilov at paras 33-64).

paragraphs.summary: Vavilov establishes presumption of reasonableness standard of review, rebuttable by legislative intent or important legal questions.

propositions.text: Applicant argues RAD decision should be reviewed on correctness standard due to natural justice violation and improper IFA test application.
propositions.quote: The Applicant argues that the impugned decision should be reviewed on the correctness standard because the RAD decision violates the principles of natural justice and does not adhere to the proper test for the determination of whether a viable IFA exists.

propositions.text: Applicant contends RAD's IFA analysis was speculative and incomplete, raising general questions of law of central importance.
propositions.quote: In essence, the Applicant argues that the RAD conducted a speculative and incomplete analysis of his persecution claims concerning Islamabad that raises “general questions of law of central importance to the legal system as a whole” citing Vavilov at paras 53, 58-59.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues RAD decision should be reviewed on correctness standard due to natural justice violation and speculative IFA analysis.

propositions.text: Court finds RAD identified and followed appropriate test for viable IFA and issues do not engage questions of central legal importance.
propositions.quote: First, I find that the RAD did identify and follow the appropriate test in its review and determination with respect to a viable IFA. These are issues that do not engage with questions of central importance to the legal system, as the decision involves specific issues that most directly affected the Applicant.

propositions.text: Court finds no procedural fairness lack attributable to RAD and issue arises within RAD's delegated authority.
propositions.quote: In addition, I am not convinced that there was any lack of procedural fairness attributable to the RAD. In my view, the general points of contention in this case relate to the RAD’s inquiry into the availability of an IFA. This type of issue is one that arises within the context of the RAD’s delegated authority (Vavilov at para 30).

propositions.text: Issue must be examined under reasonableness standard per Vavilov.
propositions.quote: Consequently, this issue must be examined according to a reasonableness standard (Vavilov at paras 73-143).

paragraphs.summary: Court finds RAD applied correct test, no procedural fairness breach, and reasonableness standard applies to IFA issue.

propositions.text: IFA question is essential to refugee system and ensures international refugee law backs up national protection when inadequate.
propositions.quote: The question of whether an IFA exists is an essential component of the refugee system. The IFA concept flows from the definition of convention refugee and helps ensure that international refugee law serves as a backup to the national protection when such protection is inadequate

paragraphs.summary: Court states IFA question is essential to refugee system and international law backup to national protection.

propositions.text: IFA concept ensures persecuted individuals seek protection within their own country before international refugee system.
propositions.quote: the IFA concept helps ensure that persecuted individuals first approach their own country before seeking protection through the international refugee system (Canada (Attorney General) v Ward, 1993 CanLII 105 (SCC), [1993] 2 SCR 689 at para 18).

paragraphs.summary: IFA concept ensures persecuted persons seek protection within their country before international refugee system.

propositions.text: RAD found Applicant safe in Islamabad with no evidence of persecution agents pursuing him and ability to earn a living.
propositions.quote: The RAD found that the Applicant’s safety would be assured in Islamabad and that it would not be unreasonable for him to seek refuge there. In particular, the RAD concluded that there was no evidence that the alleged agents of persecution would pursue him in Islamabad , and that the Applicant could earn a living there as a businessperson.

propositions.text: RAD confirmed RPD’s conclusion that an IFA was available to the Applicant based on these factors.
propositions.quote: On the basis of these factors, the RAD confirmed the RPD’s conclusion that an IFA was available to the Applicant.

paragraphs.summary: RAD found Applicant safe in Islamabad and confirmed RPD's IFA availability conclusion.

propositions.text: Two-prong IFA test requires no serious persecution possibility and unreasonableness to seek refuge in IFA area.
propositions.quote: this Court established a two-prong test to be applied in determining whether there is an IFA. Under the two-prong IFA test, it is required that: there is no serious possibility of the individual being persecuted in the IFA area (on the balance of probabilities); and conditions in the proposed IFA must be such that it would not be unreasonable in all the circumstances for an individual to seek refuge there

propositions.text: Both prongs must be satisfied for IFA finding; ensures compliance with international norms.
propositions.quote: Both prongs must be satisfied for a finding that the claimant has an IFA. This two-prong test ensures that Canada complies with international norms regarding IFAs

paragraphs.summary: Two-prong IFA test requires no serious persecution risk and unreasonableness to seek refuge; both must be met for IFA finding.

propositions.text: Two-prong IFA test ensures compliance with international norms regarding IFAs.
propositions.quote: This two-prong test ensures that Canada complies with international norms regarding IFAs (UNHCR Guidelines on International Protection at paras 7, 24-30).

paragraphs.summary: Two-prong IFA test ensures compliance with international norms regarding IFAs.

propositions.text: Gallo Farias checklist clarifies IFA availability case law with six legal criteria including notice, two-step test, burden of proof, high threshold, accessibility, and no need for friends.
propositions.quote: Mister Justice Kelen provided a “checklist of legal criteria” that further clarifies this Court’s case law on the availability of an IFA: 1. If IFA will be an issue, the Refugee Board must give notice to the refugee claimant prior to the hearing ... 6. The fact that the refugee claimant has no friends or relatives in the proposed IFA does not make the proposed IFA unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: Gallo Farias checklist clarifies IFA availability law with six criteria including notice, burden, accessibility, and reasonableness.

propositions.text: Applicant submits RAD erred on both prongs of Rasaratnam-Thirunavukkarasu IFA test.
propositions.quote: The Applicant submits that the RAD committed errors in respect of both prongs of the Rasaratnam-Thironavukkarasu test.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant submits RAD erred on both prongs of IFA test.

propositions.text: Applicant argues RAD's finding that agents of persecution no longer interested conflicts with viable IFA finding, as RAD speculated on risk existence.
propositions.quote: Applicant submits that the RAD committed an error when it determined that the agents of persecution are no longer interested in harming the Applicant, and yet also determined that there existed a viable IFA. There is an inconsistency, argues the Applicant, in the analysis as the RAD only speculated as to whether the threat continued to exist; the Applicant argues that one cannot speculate as to the existence of such a risk and then find that an available IFA exists.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues RAD's finding of no ongoing persecution risk conflicts with viable IFA finding due to speculation.

propositions.text: Court rejects Applicant's argument, finding RAD analyzed risk and concluded no risk of persecution or threat to life in Pakistan.
propositions.quote: I do not accept the Applicant’s argument. The RAD clearly, at the outset, analyzed the determination of risk and concluded that no such risk of persecution or threat to life continued to exist in the event the Applicant was to return to Pakistan .

paragraphs.summary: Court rejects Applicant's argument, finding RAD concluded no persecution risk in Pakistan.

propositions.text: RAD assumed risk continued for IFA review purpose, stating even if assault and threat occurred, IFA in Islamabad would still exist.
propositions.quote: the RAD stated: “even if the panel had believed that the claimant had been assaulted and threatened in the manner alleged, which is not the case, it would still have rejected this refugee claim because it would have assessed that the claimant would have had an internal flight alternative (IFA) in his country, in particular in the capital city Islamabad.”

paragraphs.summary: RAD assumed risk continued for IFA review, stating IFA in Islamabad would still exist even if assault occurred.

propositions.text: Court finds RAD did not speculate but assumed risk for IFA determination, no inconsistency in IFA analysis.
propositions.quote: Consequently, the RAD did not speculate, but only assumed, for the purpose of determining the existence of a viable IFA, that the risk continued to exist. I see nothing wrong with that approach, as it did not result, as is suggested by the Applicant, in an inconsistency in the IFA analysis by the RPD.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds RAD assumed risk for IFA determination and no inconsistency in IFA analysis.

propositions.text: Applicant argues RAD's finding of Islamabad as IFA was a 'knee jerk' reaction unsupported by analysis.
propositions.quote: The crux of the Applicant’s argument is that the finding that Islamabad offered an IFA was but a “knee jerk” reaction, unsupported by any analysis as to its viability.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues RAD's Islamabad IFA finding was a 'knee jerk' reaction without analysis.

propositions.text: Applicant was given full opportunity to challenge Islamabad as IFA per Gallo Farias.
propositions.quote: in accordance with Gallo Farias (at para 34), the Applicant was given a full opportunity to challenge the suitability of Islamabad as an IFA.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Applicant had full opportunity to challenge Islamabad as IFA.

propositions.text: RPD identified Islamabad as acceptable IFA location where Applicant not at risk of persecution.
propositions.quote: From the audio recording of the Applicant’s hearing before the RPD, it is clear that the RPD first identified Islamabad as an acceptable IFA location, where the Applicant would not be exposed to a risk of persecution

paragraphs.summary: RPD identified Islamabad as acceptable IFA location with no persecution risk.

propositions.text: RPD asked Applicant about living in Islamabad; Applicant said scared in Karachi but did not specifically say about Islamabad safety, claimed countrywide threat.
propositions.quote: During the interview, the RPD member asked the Applicant why he left to go to Karachi , and whether he could live elsewhere in Pakistan such as Islamabad . The Applicant responded that he tried to resettle in Karachi but that he was scared that the persecutors would kill him. The Applicant did not specifically respond as to whether he could or could not live in Islamabad , but did claim that he would not be safe anywhere in Pakistan due to the agents of persecution’s countrywide network.

paragraphs.summary: RPD questioned Applicant about Islamabad; Applicant feared Karachi but did not specifically deny Islamabad safety, claimed countrywide threat.

propositions.text: Threatening calls and friend's affidavit show continued risk of persecution even in Islamabad
propositions.quote: the threatening telephone calls received by the Applicant while he was living in Karachi , as well as his friend’s affidavit confirming that the assailants were still returning to the Applicant’s business in Sahiwal, demonstrate the continued nature of his risk of persecution, even in Islamabad .

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues threatening calls and affidavit show continued persecution risk even in Islamabad.

propositions.text: Pakistani police inefficiency and possible complicity undermine IFA viability due to risk of location leaks
propositions.quote: documentary evidence suggests that the Pakistani police force is inefficient, corrupt, and may be complicit with the persecuting organizations. Counsel postulated that certain members of the police force could leak the Applicant’s location to the persecutors. According to the Applicant’s counsel, the possibility of a leak undermines the possibility of an IFA.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant's counsel argues police corruption risks location leaks, undermining IFA viability.

propositions.text: RAD found persecutors uninterested in Islamabad due to closed drugstore and lack of evidence of intent to find Applicant there
propositions.quote: The RAD determined that the agents of persecution had no interest in chasing the Applicant to Islamabad since his drugstore was closed and he stopped selling contraceptives. The RAD also noted that the Applicant had failed to provide evidence as to the aggressors’ ability or intentions to find him in Islamabad .

paragraphs.summary: RAD found persecutors uninterested in Islamabad and Applicant failed to show aggressors' intent to find him there.

propositions.text: RAD found Applicant could avoid threatening calls by changing phone number and no evidence of assailants' location or knowledge of Applicant's whereabouts in Karachi
propositions.quote: the RAD determined that the Applicant could avoid these types of calls by changing his telephone number from the one he used for his drugstore. In any event, there was no evidence as to where the assailants were calling from, or that they knew that the Applicant was in Karachi at the time of the call.

paragraphs.summary: RAD found Applicant could avoid calls by changing number; no evidence of assailants' location or knowledge of Applicant in Karachi.

propositions.text: RAD found assailants unaware of Applicant's whereabouts and lack of threats to family shows little interest in targeting Applicant
propositions.quote: The RAD determined that the friend’s report indicating that the assailants were returning to the Applicant’s former drugstore looking for him simply shows that the aggressors were unaware of the Applicant’s whereabouts. The RAD also determined that the lack of threats directed against the Applicant’s spouse and children in Karachi or his father and siblings in Sahiwal shows that the aggressors have little interest in targeting the Applicant.

propositions.text: Mere suspicions of being hunted in home country insufficient to preclude acceptable IFA location
propositions.quote: Mere suspicions of being hunted in one’s home country is insufficient to preclude an otherwise acceptable IFA location (Kumar v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2012 FC 30 at para 35).

paragraphs.summary: RAD found assailants unaware of Applicant's location and little interest in targeting him; mere suspicions insufficient to preclude IFA.

propositions.text: RAD ruled Applicant failed to show unacceptable risk in proposed IFA, burden on Applicant
propositions.quote: the RAD ruled that the Applicant had not discharged his burden to show that relocation to the proposed IFA would expose him to an unacceptable risk (Gallo Farias at para 23; Thirunavukkarasu at para 12; Mwaura v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2008 FC 748 at para 13; Whenu v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2003 FC 1041 at para 11).

paragraphs.summary: RAD ruled Applicant failed to show unacceptable risk in IFA; burden on Applicant.

propositions.text: RAD found insufficient evidence of persecution risk in Islamabad
propositions.quote: the Applicant failed to provide sufficient evidence as to his risk of persecution in Islamabad .

propositions.text: Court finds RAD's findings on persecution risk in Islamabad reasonable and will not disturb them
propositions.quote: I see nothing unreasonable about the RAD’s findings on this issue, and thus no reason to disturb the RAD’s determination under the first prong of the Rasaratnam-Thironavukkarasu test.

paragraphs.summary: RAD found insufficient evidence of persecution risk in Islamabad; Court finds RAD's findings reasonable and will not disturb them.

propositions.text: Applicant argues RAD's second prong analysis incomplete, failing to address full range of issues for refuge in Islamabad
propositions.quote: the Applicant submits that the RAD’s analysis under the second prong of the Rasaratnam-Thironavukkarasu test was incomplete because it failed to address the full range of issues in determining whether, even if the first prong was met, it was reasonable for the Applicant to seek refuge in Islamabad .

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues RAD's second prong analysis incomplete, missing full range of issues for refuge in Islamabad.

propositions.text: Applicant says RAD only considered work and housing, should have addressed transportation, language, education, accommodation, religion, indigenous status, healthcare
propositions.quote: the Applicant submits that the RAD should have addressed the full range of issues related to the IFA location, namely, transportation and travel, language, education, accommodation, religion, indigenous status and the availability of healthcare.

propositions.text: Applicant cites RAD case lacking legal basis for enumerated factors, claims RAD unjustifiably omitted these issues
propositions.quote: In support of this argument, the Applicant cites a case from the RAD, one that does not cite a legal basis for the enumerated factors. The Applicant believes that the RAD unjustifiably omitted to address these issues.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant says RAD only considered work and housing, should have addressed many factors; cites RAD case lacking legal basis, claims omission unjustified.

propositions.text: RAD claimed Applicant did not contest RPD's second prong analysis
propositions.quote: the RAD claimed that the Applicant did not contest the RPD’s analysis under the second prong.

propositions.text: Applicant says RAD misconstrued his appeal memorandum, which challenges RPD's lack of analysis on state protection in Islamabad
propositions.quote: To the Applicant, this justification misconstrues the written argumentation in his appeal memorandum, wherein he challenges the RPD’s lack of analysis as to the sufficiency of state protection in Islamabad .

paragraphs.summary: RAD said Applicant did not contest RPD's second prong; Applicant says RAD misconstrued his memorandum challenging state protection analysis.

propositions.text: Respondent agrees RAD need not address each factor as second prong uncontested and no evidence shows unreasonableness
propositions.quote: The Respondent agrees with the RAD, and argues that it was unnecessary to address each factor because the second prong of the test was uncontested by the Applicant. Moreover, the Respondent argues that the Applicant has not provided any evidence that shows how the substance of the RAD’s determination was unreasonable under the second prong of the test.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent agrees RAD need not address each factor as second prong uncontested and no evidence shows unreasonableness.

propositions.text: Court rejects Applicant's arguments for four reasons
propositions.quote: I reject the Applicant’s arguments for four reasons.

paragraphs.summary: Court rejects Applicant's arguments for four reasons.

propositions.text: Applicant did not raise 'range of issues' argument at RAD despite burden to show IFA unsuitability
propositions.quote: the Applicant’s argument regarding the ‘range of issues’ under the second prong was not raised at the RAD level. The Applicant did not raise such arguments in his memorandum at the RAD, despite the Applicant’s burden of proof to demonstrate how a proposed IFA would be unsuitable.

propositions.text: Applicant only challenged RPD's state protection analysis, which relates to first prong
propositions.quote: Indeed, the Applicant merely challenges the RPD’s analysis as to the level of state protection in Islamabad , a consideration that relates to the first prong of the Rasaratnam-Thironavukkarasu test (i.e., the analysis pertaining to the fear of persecution).

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Applicant did not raise 'range of issues' at RAD and only challenged RPD's state protection analysis related to first prong.

propositions.text: Applicant's RAD memorandum omits factors like transportation, language, education, accommodation, religion, indigenous status, healthcare
propositions.quote: The Applicant’s memorandum before the RAD does not mention the factors of transportation and travel, language, education, accommodation, religion, indigenous status and the availability of healthcare.

propositions.text: Applicant attempts to raise new legal issues that could have been raised before judicial review
propositions.quote: As a result, the Applicant is attempting to raise new legal issues that could have been raised prior to this judicial review (Alberta (Information and Privacy Commissioner) v Alberta Teachers’ Association, 2011 SCC 61 at paras 22-26; Forest Ethics Advocacy Association v Canada (National Energy Board), [2015] 4 FCR 75, 2014 FCA 245 at paras 42-47; Erasmo v Canada (Attorney General), 2015 FCA 129 at para 33).

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Applicant's RAD memorandum omits key factors and attempts to raise new legal issues too late.

propositions.text: Applicant misconstrues IFA claim nature by requiring full analysis of categorized factors
propositions.quote: the Applicant misconstrues the nature of an IFA claim in requiring a full analysis of certain categorized factors.

propositions.text: Second prong's 'reasonable in all circumstances' standard is high, fact-sensitive, requiring concrete evidence of jeopardizing conditions
propositions.quote: The “reasonable in all the circumstances” standard (of the second prong of the Rasaratnam-Thironavukkarasu test) is a high threshold that cannot be defined in an abstract manner. That standard requires “nothing less than the existence of conditions which would jeopardize the life and safety of a claimant in travelling or temporarily relocating to a safe area” as well as “actual and concrete evidence of such conditions.” (Ranganathan v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), [2001] 2 FC 164, 2000 CanLII 16789 (FCA) at para 15, referring to Thirunavukkarasu at 597, 599).

propositions.text: Relevant conditions and evidence vary case by case; Applicant's argument would confine inquiry and shift burden to tribunal
propositions.quote: The relevant “conditions” and types of relevant “evidence” vary from case to case. If accepted, the Applicant’s argument would confine this fact-sensitive inquiry and transfer the burden of proof to the tribunal. These consequences would frustrate the contextual, case-by-case nature of the test.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Applicant misconstrues IFA claim nature; second prong is high, fact-sensitive standard requiring concrete evidence; Applicant's argument would wrongly shift burden.

propositions.text: Applicant provided no evidence or substantive argument on Islamabad's inability to provide adequate services
propositions.quote: The Applicant has not provided evidence or made a substantive argument as to Islamabad ’s inability to provide adequate employment, shelter, transportation, education, healthcare, and services adapted to the Applicant’s situation (e.g., language, religion, indigenous status).

propositions.text: Applicant faults RAD for not assessing IFA suitability, but burden lies with Applicant to show undue hardship
propositions.quote: Instead, the Applicant tries to fault the RAD for not taking upon itself this task. Again, the burden to show how a proposed IFA location is unsuitable lies with the Applicant – not the RAD. It is the Applicant’s burden to show how relocation would cause him an undue hardship in the light of the Applicant’s particular situation and objective information related to the proposed IFA location (e.g., Okonkwo v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2019 FC 1330 at para 17).

paragraphs.summary: Applicant gave no evidence on Islamabad's inadequacy and wrongly faults RAD; burden to show hardship lies with Applicant.

propositions.text: Applicant asks Court to reweigh evidence under second prong, which is not Court's role in judicial review
propositions.quote: the Applicant is essentially asking this Court to reweigh the evidence under this second prong; that is not the role of the Court in judicial review proceedings (Vavilov at para 125; Akinfolajimi v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2018 FC 722 at paras 27-28; Titcombe at para 22; Khosa at para 61).

paragraphs.summary: Applicant asks Court to reweigh evidence under second prong; Court says this is not its role in judicial review.

propositions.text: Application for judicial review is dismissed; no question for certification
propositions.quote: The application for judicial review is dismissed. There is no question for certification.

paragraphs.summary: Court dismisses judicial review application and finds no question for certification.
